Topics.
The Four Quarters: Cost of Delivery (COGS + Shipping), CAC (Variable Marketing), OPEX (Fixed Costs), Profit.
Cost of Delivery: Target 30-40%.
OPEX Scaling: Target 10-12%. Rule: Base full-time payroll at 12% of the absolute lowest revenue month of the year; everything above that is flex/variable labor.
Cash Flow vs. P&L: Trading P&L margin for cash velocity (e.g., liquidating aged inventory below cost to free up working capital).
Vendor as Lender: Negotiating net terms (Net 60, Net 90, Net 120) aligned with the manufacturing timeline so inventory is sold before the invoice is paid.

Look for. Strict definitions of where specific costs sit. For instance, distinguishing between a variable creative expense (CAC) and a fixed agency retainer (OPEX). Look for the exact baseline metrics for OPEX (10-12%) and Cost of Delivery (30-40%).
Skip. General adages about "saving money" or basic accounting principles not specific to the four-quarter DTC model.
Scope mix. 80% baseline (structuring the math), 20% growth (leveraging terms for capital). Volume. ~500 words.

Topics.
The Pyramid: 1. Contribution Margin (Top), 2. Business Metrics (Revenue, Spend, blended MER), 3. Customer Metrics (New vs. Returning), 4. Channel Level (ROAS, in-platform proxy metrics).

Daily Contribution Margin: The primary daily focus for the team: Net Sales minus Product Cost minus Variable Expense minus Ad Spend. Fixed costs (OPEX) are excluded from the daily view to prevent false signals to cut spend.
Returns Accrual: Applying an estimated return rate to current daily revenue rather than processing cash-basis returns, preventing false negative signals in high-return months like January.
Measurement and Optimization: Why MTA (Multi-Touch Attribution) models matter less than the signal passed back to the Meta algorithm. You must optimize for what the platform uses to allocate dollars.

Channel Expansion Measurement: When moving beyond Meta to YouTube/CTV/TikTok, measurement must expand beyond .com to include Amazon/Retail lift. E.g., YouTube drives almost 1:1 value on Amazon as it does on .com.
Look for. The explicit formula for Contribution Margin. The specific rules for when to run incrementality tests (when expanding beyond a single channel like Meta).
Skip. Generic platform setup guides (how to launch a Facebook campaign).
Scope mix. 90% baseline (setting the rules). Volume. ~600 words.

url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RHJSO4eVJVA rights: public_reference why: Shifts e-commerce growth from a media buying problem to a merchandising and demand-creation problem. modules: [03-MER] topics: [Product Development, Demand Creation, Marketing Calendar, Merchandising] tier: 3 scope_hint: growth
Topics.

Progressive Peaking: Engineering four distinct peaks a year (one per quarter). Creating a cultural or narrative reason for a consumer to buy today, increasing conversion rates while holding CPMs constant. E.g., attaching to International Women's Day or Veterans Day to spike demand outside of BFCM.
Product MVP Matrix: Evaluating SKUs by Margin Expansion, Volume Velocity, or Cash Flow correction.
The Four SKU Types:
Champions: High volume, high efficiency.
Growth Drivers: Increasing investment to find the ceiling.
Hidden Gems: Low investment, disproportionately high efficiency (needs more spend).
Underperformers (Aged Inventory): Liquidate quickly to recover cash.

De-risking Category Expansion: Using small-batch manufacturing or pre-orders to validate demand before committing media budget or large POs. Mapping the required media spend before placing the inventory order.
Look for. The criteria for defining a "peak." The criteria for categorizing a SKU into one of the four types (Champions, Gems, etc.).
Skip. General advice on "listening to your customer" for product ideas.
Scope mix. 30% baseline, 70% growth. Volume. ~600 words.
